blocks.x: Hilary, a 39-year-old in California, has had depression for about as long as she can remember, which means she’s tried a lot of antidepressants. Mostly, though, the meds left her unimpressed.

Last year, she started taking the GLP-1 medication Wegovy to lose weight. Right away, she felt some of her sadness lifting. After months on a GLP-1, she felt like her entire outlook had become more positive. No one was more surprised than Hilary. “I didn’t even know it was possible for GLP-1s to have a positive effect on mental illness until it happened to me,” she says.

Hilary had accidentally stumbled into a cutting edge—and somewhat controversial—corner of psychiatry. In recent years a growing number of doctors have acknowledged that what you eat can affect how you feel, giving rise to the world of food therapy and nutritional psychiatry. Now a small group is taking that concept further, betting that GLP-1s, medications that have fundamentally changed how Americans eat, may also have major benefits for mental health.

Since well before everyone was on Ozempic, research published in journals like Translational Psychiatry and Diabetes Care has shown that health issues including obesity, high blood sugar, poor gut health, and chronic inflammation often go along with mental illness. When people improve their diets, their mental health sometimes gets better—perhaps because some of those physical health issues improve, translating to benefits for the brain. When about 20 people with depression cut back on processed foods for a month, they felt happier and less anxious, according to an experiment published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) Psychiatry in September.

Providers like Joanna Buck, a Wisconsin psychiatrist, have started using brain-friendly diets as a supplement to traditional therapy. “More than just taking a pill or taking a medication or an injection, [a dietary approach] can really provide benefits to the person as a whole,” Buck says.

GLP-1s have a profound effect on weight, metabolic health, and inflammation, beyond what many people can accomplish with diet changes alone. Could these drugs supercharge the effects of nutritional psychiatry? Some doctors think so.

Thomas Rutledge, who spent more than two decades as a University of California, San Diego professor and in-house psychologist for a California Veteran Affairs weight-control clinic, thinks it’s possible. He noticed an obvious change in his patients when GLP-1s began sweeping the nation. They were typically using the medications for weight loss or diabetes treatment, but sometimes getting more than they bargained for, including “life-changing” mental health benefits. “We had people who responded tremendously, better than they had to any psychiatric medicine or psychotherapy they’d ever tried,” he says.

Not everyone got better, Rutledge is quick to note, and some actually got worse. But in a study Rutledge published in the medical journal Heart and Mind this year, he found that in a sample size of 40 people, severity of depression dropped by 30% within six months of starting a GLP-1, on average. Other studies have also found that these meds can help treat depression, bipolar, and more, and pharma giant Eli Lilly and Company is even studying a not-yet-released GLP-1 for depression.

Rutledge thinks the drugs may be helpful, in part, because they set off a positive domino effect involving metabolic health improvements, increased energy, and better food choices. By contrast, many traditional psychiatric drugs slow one’s metabolism or cause weight gain, leading some psychiatrists to use GLP-1s to undo the damage.

The meds’ well-documented ability to quiet obsessive thoughts about food, or “food noise,” may also hold clues about why they’re helpful on the therapy couch. It’s possible they disrupt the strong, repetitive thought patterns seen among people with addiction, some studies suggest.

The preliminary results are promising but GLP-1s are not currently approved as mental health treatments. In fact, some research, like a 2024 study in Scientific Reports, raised concerns that GLP-1s may lead to higher risks of psychiatric illnesses like depression and anxiety, as well as suicidal behavior. Studies can come to different conclusions depending on how they’re designed—but, encouragingly, recent reviews synthesizing many different studies on GLP-1s like one in JAMA Psychiatry have generally not found reason for alarm.

For a while, some of the drugs’ packaging carried warnings about potential suicide risk. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) told manufacturers to remove those warnings in January, saying its review of the science did not find evidence that GLP-1s cause self-harm, depression, psychosis, or other mental health problems.

Still, some mental health professionals are wary. While Buck incorporates food into her practice, she doesn’t feel comfortable adding GLP-1s to the menu just yet. “Time will tell, as it always does, whether or not we’re heading in the right direction or if the train is going too fast,” she says.

Rutledge agrees that a lot more research is needed and says there are real risks when using these medications without proper care and monitoring. “At this point, they’re still not going to be a front-line medicine that a psychiatrist is likely to consider,” he says.
“But very likely in the future,” that will change, he says. “It’s probably already beginning.”
